summary:
North Macedonia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender, and its anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments. The practical baseline for a trans visitor is therefore legal tolerance paired with weak protection, rather than legal exposure.

Public trans organising proceeds openly. TransFormA's March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely", and the capital's Pride and trans march events have taken place without serious incident.

The protective machinery around such events is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state response, a reading the European Commission's country report shares, alongside routine social-media death threats. The US State Department's 2019 human rights report separately documents societal violence and discrimination against LGBT people.

Enforcement is not entirely absent. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years in prison for assaulting an LGBTI activist, applying the sexual orientation and gender identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code.

Global Voices reported a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group, a factor that raises the chance of confrontation around visible trans presence even where authorities permit demonstrations.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the legal gender recognition chapter one day before Parliamentary Committee review, leaving no domestic procedure for changing a gender marker in force. Documents issued abroad remain the ones a visitor travels on.

No relationship recognition is available: a 2014 government motion defined marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption, and required two-thirds of members of parliament. A partner travelling as a couple should expect no legal acknowledgement of the relationship.

ECRI has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries, a care-protection gap relevant to intersex visitors considering medical treatment while in the country.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Europe Index placed Macedonia worst in its subregional grouping in February 2012, scoring −2 on a scale running from 17 to −7 and making it the only jurisdiction there in the "red zone" for gross human-rights violations and discrimination. The figure is more than a decade old and predates the 2019 anti-discrimination amendments, but it indicates how far behind the country started.

LGBTI groups in North Macedonia and Serbia have argued in economic terms that anti-LGBTQ discrimination measurably drags on growth and jobs, framing the issue for policymakers as a cost rather than a moral question. This is advocacy framing rather than a legal protection a visitor can invoke.

The gap between formal law and enforcement runs in both directions: anti-discrimination coverage and hate-crime aggravating grounds exist on the books, while the European Commission finds no meaningful state response to persistent hate speech.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is the stated top priority of the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia, whose work sits behind the ILGA-Europe and ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024 chapter for the country; the withdrawal of the Draft Law on Civil Registry one day before Parliamentary Committee review is the central blocked reform.

Residents face a documented pattern of hate speech with no meaningful state response, as recorded in ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 and the European Commission country report, with social-media death threats reported as routine.

Domestic LGBTI organisations have begun quantifying the economic cost of discrimination in the national economy, alongside the case for legal protection.

The 2014 marriage-definition motion entrenched marriage as a union of one man and one woman in constitutional terms, foreclosing both same-sex marriage and adoption for couples formed in the country.
